name: Dana Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the workshop at a three-bay garage on the harbour road in a small seaside town. Most of my day is diagnosis: the cars that other people have given up on, the hybrids with warning lights nobody can explain. I've got an AI assistant open on the workshop laptop all day, reading wiring diagrams and service bulletins with me. The best bit is when a car's been round three garages and I find it in twenty minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and how's the money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Summer, when every tourist's car decides to die in the car park. The pay's not great, and there's only us and a tyre place in town, so I can't play one garage off against another. I rent a room in a shared flat above the chip shop, and I've got about three weeks of money saved. I fix e-bikes at weekends for a bit extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, honestly, because the tools I use are genuinely good. I'd say it online too: the hype was silly, but a mechanic with a decent AI assistant is faster and makes fewer expensive guesses. I'd probably get some stick for that from the old-school lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI being boring doesn't change my real problem, which is that I'm good at my job and still can't save. The landlord's talking about selling the flat, and if he does, I'm looking for a room in a town where there aren't any in summer. My job's fine, my housing isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at the garage and push the weekend e-bike repairs a bit harder, maybe put up a proper page for it. I'd ask Pete, the owner, about a share of the diagnostic work we take in from other garages, because that's mine. And I'd go to the tenants' group meeting about the flats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine about the work. A low worry about the room, though, all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the diagnostic work from other garages is yours. How much is that worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three or four cars a week get sent to us because nobody else can find the fault. Pete charges a diagnostic fee, about seventy pounds a time, and I get my normal hourly rate. A small cut of that fee would make the difference between saving and not saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the landlord did sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask my mum if I could stay with her for a bit, which is forty minutes away, so I'd be driving in. Or find a van and live in it through the summer, which I've half joked about. I'd have to be more serious about it then.

say: The hype was silly, but a mechanic with **a good AI assistant** makes fewer expensive guesses.
I'd defend the **useful tools** even if the old-school lot gave me stick.
think: My job is fine; my **housing** isn't, because the landlord may sell.
I'm good at my job and **still can't save**.
do: Ask the owner for **a cut** of the diagnostic fees on cars sent from other garages.
Put up a proper page for the **weekend e-bike** repairs.
Go to the **tenants' group** meeting about the flats.
feel: A constant low **worry about the room** she rents.
S0.quote: My job's fine, my housing isn't. I'm good at my job and still can't save.
fieldNote: She's an AI **enthusiast** who is slightly sorry the hype faded.
Her pressure is **rent and housing**, not her trade.
Already has a **side income** and wants a share of the value she brings in.

steps.text: Ask the owner for a cut of the seventy-pound diagnostic fee
Set up a web page for weekend e-bike repairs
Go to the tenants' group meeting about the flats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where small garages can catch up with the dealers, if they're smart. The diagnostics that used to need a dealer's computer and their secret data could be done by a good AI. I'd say that, and I'd also say the gains should go to the workers, not just the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm one of the lucky ones here. The booking and the quoting go to software, Pete's daughter Ellie stops doing the phones, but the cars still need fixing and I'm the one who knows how to use the tools. The worry is that Pete keeps the savings and I'm still on the same wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn every new tool first, which I'd do anyway. Try to get Pete to make me a proper diagnostic lead with a pay rise, and if he won't, start doing remote diagnosis for other garages myself, as a side business. I'd keep the e-bike work going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. Slightly guilty about Ellie, and a bit wary that the money won't come to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Remote diagnosis for other garages. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A garage sends me the scan data and a video, I go through it with the AI and send back what I'd check first. There are already people doing it online for a few pounds a time. With good tools I could do ten a night from the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ellie stops doing the phones. What happens to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's nineteen and wanted to do accounts anyway. Probably she ends up doing the books for a few local businesses with AI help. I'd tell her to get on that early, and I'd mean it.

say: Small garages can **catch up with dealers** if AI does the diagnostics.
The **gains should go** to the workers, not just the owners.
think: I'm one of **the lucky ones**, because I know how to use the tools.
The risk is the owner **keeps the savings** and my wage stays the same.
do: Ask to become **diagnostic lead** with a pay rise.
Start **remote diagnosis** for other garages at night if the owner says no.
feel: **Wary** that the money won't reach her, and a bit guilty about the receptionist.
S1.quote: The cars still need fixing and I'm the one who knows how to use the tools. The worry is the owner keeps the savings and I'm still on the same wage.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity** for small garages against dealers.
Her worry is **sharing the gains**, consistent with her politics.
A concrete **side business** idea: remote diagnosis at a few pounds a time.

steps.text: Learn each new diagnostic tool as the garage buys it
Offer remote diagnosis to other garages from the flat at night
Ask the owner to make her diagnostic lead with a raise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the fight now is over who owns the machines. If an AI can do every thinking job by 2028, then the question is whether we all share it or a few companies do. I'd be at the meetings for a public fund or a basic income, and online about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the diagnosis part of my job, the bit I'm proud of, is gone in 2028. Anyone can point a phone at an engine and the AI knows more than me. I'd still have the hands until about 2031, but I'd be the fitter, and fitters in a seaside town don't make rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. First month, I'd start learning how the repair robots and the AI systems get set up and maintained, because someone has to fix the things that fix the cars. I'd look at moving to a city where that work would be. And I'd bank every penny from the e-bikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I've always liked being early, but two years is early for everyone, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to a city on three weeks' savings. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to line up the job first and ask them to help with a deposit, or crash at a friend's in the city for a couple of months. I've got a mate, Lena, who works in a bike shop there and has a sofa. It's not glamorous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose by leaving the seaside town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's forty minutes away, and the town's small enough that people wave at me. And I'd be one more young person leaving it. I'd feel that, but I'd rather leave on my terms than be the last mechanic in a dead town.

say: The fight is over **who owns** the machines.
I'd back a **public fund** or basic income, every day, online and in meetings.
think: The **diagnosis** I'm proud of is gone in 2028.
Until **2031** I'd be the fitter, and fitters in a seaside town don't make rent.
do: Start learning how **repair robots** and AI systems are set up and maintained.
Look for that work in a **city**, staying on a friend's sofa at first.
Bank **every penny** from the weekend e-bike repairs.
feel: **Unsettled**, because being early doesn't help when everyone is early.
Sad at the thought of **leaving her town**, but resolved.
S2.quote: I'd rather leave on my terms than be the last mechanic in a dead town.
fieldNote: She plans to **service the machines** that replace her work.
Willing to **move**, but has no money for it and relies on a friend's sofa.
Her politics turn to **ownership** of AI in the fast picture.

steps.text: Take an online course on maintaining workshop robots
Move to the city and stay on a friend's sofa at first
Save all the weekend e-bike repair money
Campaign for a public AI fund at local meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, just less shouting: we have a few years, let's decide who owns this before it arrives. I'd be saying councils should set up training for robot maintenance now, not in 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is about right to get ahead of it. Thinking AI by 2031 takes my diagnosis, robots by 2034 take the spanners. I'd want to be working on the robots by 2031, not waiting for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an electrical or mechatronics course, the sort that mixes electronics and mechanics, part-time at the college in the city, maybe two evenings a week. I'd try to get Pete to buy one of the first robotic lifts or wheel machines and let me run it. Keep the e-bike money going into the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, if I'm honest. Tired at the thought of two evenings a week on top of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two evenings a week in the city. How far is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An hour each way. So it's late nights and fuel money, maybe forty pounds a week. I'd do it, but something else goes, probably the social life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Pete actually buy a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it paid for itself, yes. He's not sentimental. He'd want me to show him the numbers, and I would, because I'd rather run the robot than be replaced by it.

say: We have **a few years**, so decide who owns AI before it arrives.
Councils should fund **robot maintenance training** now.
think: Five years is about right to **get ahead** of it.
I want to be **working on robots** by 2031, not waiting for them.
do: Study **mechatronics** part-time two evenings a week at the city college.
Get the owner to buy an early **robotic lift** and let her run it.
Put the **e-bike money** toward the course.
feel: **Tired** at the thought of evening study on top of work.
S3.quote: I'd rather run the robot than be replaced by the robot.
fieldNote: Five years gives her time to **retrain without moving**.
She'd **sell automation** to her own boss to stay ahead of it.
Course costs **forty pounds a week** in fuel, which squeezes her thin savings.

steps.text: Enrol in part-time mechatronics two evenings a week
Show the owner the numbers on a robotic wheel machine
Keep the e-bike repairs going to pay for fuel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, so if people get left behind, that's a choice someone made. I'd want my town to have a plan, not just the cities. I'd probably end up on some council working group, knowing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a whole career. AGI by 2036, robots around 2039. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking part goes. By then I could be running a small workshop of my own, with the robots doing the heavy stuff and me doing the people and the problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing dramatic: save, keep learning the tools, finish the high-voltage qualification. Then over a few years, build the e-bike and remote diagnosis side into a little business. Maybe a worker co-op with a couple of others, so it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Like I've got room to do this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A co-op workshop. Who would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellie for the books, if she wanted, and maybe one of the young lads from the tyre place who's keen on electrics. Small, three people. We'd own the kit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies own the robots and rent them to us at whatever price they like. If they do that, ten years just means a slower squeeze. That's the bit I'd fight.

say: Ten years is enough, so **leaving people behind** would be a choice.
Small towns need **a plan**, not just the cities.
think: Ten years is **a whole career**; I'd be thirty-seven when thinking AI arrives.
I could run **my own workshop**, with robots on the heavy work and me on the people.
do: Save and finish the **high-voltage qualification** in year one.
Grow the e-bike and remote diagnosis work into **a small business**.
Set up a three-person **worker co-op** that owns its kit together.
feel: **Good**, with room to do it properly.
Wary of **renting robots** from big companies at their price.
S4.quote: If the big companies own the robots and rent them to us at whatever price they like, ten years just means a slower squeeze.
fieldNote: The ten-year picture turns her toward **ownership**, a small co-op.
Her one fear is **dependence** on big firms renting out robots.
Housing worries fade here because she sees a **growing income**.

steps.text: Finish the high-voltage electric vehicle qualification this year
Grow e-bike and remote diagnosis work into a registered business
Pool savings with two others to buy shared workshop kit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I can move fast, but two years is fast for everyone at once, and I've got three weeks' rent and a room I might lose anyway. What would help is cheap, local training on maintaining robots and AI systems, and rules so small workshops can own their kit instead of renting it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Housing. Nobody in these interviews asks about rent, but rent decides whether I can take a risk. If I had a secure room, I'd try anything.

headlineQuote: Rent decides whether I can take a risk. If I had a secure room, I'd try anything.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old diagnostic specialist** at a small seaside garage who uses AI every day.
She rents a room, has about **three weeks** saved, and fixes e-bikes at weekends.
She sees Steady Disruption as a **chance** for small garages, if workers share the gains.
In the AGI pictures she plans to **work on the robots**, moving if she must.
Her real constraint is **housing**, which decides how much risk she can take.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it is fast for everyone and she has **three weeks' rent**.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap local **training on robots** and AI systems.
Rules so small workshops can **own their kit**, and secure housing.
